interviewQuestions.question: How would you implement a queue using only two stacks, and what's the actual time complexity of dequeue?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I keep an in-stack and an out-stack. Enqueue always just pushes onto the in-stack — O(1), no exceptions. Dequeue checks the out-stack first: if it has elements, pop directly from it. If it's empty, I pop everything off the in-stack and push it onto the out-stack — that single bulk transfer reverses the order, putting the oldest element on top — then pop from the out-stack.

On the complexity: a single dequeue call can be O(n) in the worst case, when a full transfer is triggered. But that's not the complete answer, and I'd say the complete one explicitly: dequeue is **O(1) amortized**. The argument is that every element is pushed onto the in-stack once, transferred to the out-stack at most once over its entire lifetime, and popped from the out-stack once — a bounded, constant number of touches per element regardless of how many other dequeue calls happen around it. Summed across n total operations, that's O(n) total work, which is what "O(1) amortized" means.

I'd flag that answering just "O(n)" or just "O(1)" alone is incomplete — the honest answer needs both numbers, worst-case-per-call and amortized-per-call, because they tell you different things about how the structure behaves under sustained use versus in a single unlucky call.

**Testing:** whether you can both implement this correctly and defend the amortized bound rigorously, which is the actual point of the question.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: How would you build a stack using queues, and how does its cost profile compare to the two-stack queue?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
One clean approach uses a single queue with rotation. Push appends the new element to the back of the queue, then rotates the whole queue — repeatedly moving front elements to the back — exactly `size - 1` times, so the newest element ends up at the front. Pop then just dequeues from the front, which is always the most recently pushed element, giving correct LIFO order.

The cost profile is the mirror image of the two-stack queue, but with an important asymmetry worth calling out: push here is O(n) on **every single call**, not amortized — the rotation happens unconditionally each time, with no rare-expensive/mostly-cheap pattern. The two-stack queue's expensive operation (the transfer) is genuinely rare relative to the number of calls, which is what makes it amortize to O(1); this rotation-based stack's expensive push doesn't have that property at all.

So while the two structures look symmetric on the surface — 'build one discipline out of the opposite one, with an O(n) cost somewhere' — their actual behavior under sustained use is quite different: one design has a genuinely good average case, the other pays O(n) every time regardless of history.

I'd mention this comparison unprompted if just asked to build the stack, since it's the natural follow-up an interviewer would otherwise ask.

**Testing:** whether you recognize that superficially symmetric designs can have meaningfully different amortized behavior.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Implementation

interviewQuestions.question: Why do interviewers ask the two-stacks-as-a-queue question so often, given the implementation itself is fairly simple?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because the implementation is the easy half — most candidates get there with a small hint. What actually separates a strong answer is the complexity analysis, specifically noticing that a `while` loop capable of running up to n times per call doesn't automatically make the whole structure O(n) per operation, and being able to prove the amortized O(1) claim rather than just assert it.

The proof structure — each element is touched a bounded, constant number of times over its entire lifetime, so total work over n operations is O(n) — is a template that shows up constantly elsewhere: it's the same reasoning that justifies why dynamic array append is O(1) amortized despite occasional O(n) resizes, why hash table insert is O(1) amortized despite occasional O(n) rehashes, and why union-find with path compression gets its near-constant-time guarantee. Interviewers who ask this question are really checking whether you have that general amortized-cost intuition, using queue-from-stacks as a small, self-contained proxy for it.

A candidate who nails the implementation but says "dequeue is O(n)" without qualification has actually missed the point of the question, even though the code they wrote is entirely correct — which is exactly why I make sure to state both the worst-case-per-call number and the amortized number explicitly, unprompted.

**Testing:** whether you understand what's actually being probed beneath the surface-level implementation task.
